reader.title: Killing of W. E. Ashley and Eugene Grove
bases: A band described as vigilantes hanged Eugene Grove at their camp and shot W. E. Ashley dead when he resisted (A1, A3, A4).

Two men were killed, one by hanging, by a band the dispatch calls vigilantes and whose act it calls murder (A1, A3); the band's size is not given and no accusation or stated reason appears, so the group size and pretext rest only on the word 'vigilantes' (A3, A5).
Every report is a copy or condensation of one Belvidere, Kan., dispatch of April 26 (A1, A3, A4, A8), and no independent local account or follow-up was found.

summary.text: The killing of W. E. Ashley and Eugene Grove was the hanging of Grove and shooting of Ashley, two men from Belvidere, Kansas, by a band of vigilantes a few miles below Englewood in the Indian Territory, reported in late April 1888.
Grove was hanged at the vigilantes' camp and Ashley was shot dead after he opened fire, while two women travelling with them were never accounted for.

A single Belvidere dispatch carried the story from Washington to the Kansas weeklies, and its closing judgment that vigilantes were "worse than those whom they seek to kill" made it a small case against frontier vigilantism.
According to the dispatch, Dr. W. E. Ashley and Eugene Grove of Belvidere hired a team and buggy to go into "the Nation" on a hunting and prospecting tour.
Two women went with them, described in the dispatch as their "companions" and in the German-language Illinois Staats-Zeitung as two young women.
No report gives the race of the travellers or of the vigilantes, and none says why the band stopped them.
A few miles below Englewood the party was met by vigilantes, who called Grove to their camp and, "without warning or ceremony," hanged him.
Copies differ on the gallows: the Wichita Eagle said a sapling, while the Washington Critic and the Springfield Daily Republic said "rails crossed on saplings."
Ashley then drew his Winchester and opened fire, and the vigilantes killed him at once, with fifteen balls reported in his body.
The sheriff, printed as Oleson in some copies and as Echolz or Echols in others, returned from the scene saying he could find no trace of the people or the team.
The dispatch said that what had become of the bodies and of the women "can not be conjectured."
No report of arrests, an inquest or the recovery of the bodies was found in the coverage.
The story first appeared in the Washington Critic on April 26 under the head "Hanged by Vigilantes" and ran the next day in the Memphis Appeal, the Wichita Eagle and the Springfield Daily Republic.

The full version closed with an editorial line calling it "the most atrocious deed" in "a country where crime has full sway," and the Springfield paper headed it "Vigilantes Kill an Estimable Citizen."
The Illinois Staats-Zeitung summarized it in German, calling the killers a gang of murderers who called themselves vigilantes.
In early May the Kansas weeklies took it up, the Emporia Weekly News as "Inhuman Vigilants" and the Western Kansas World as "Two Kansas Men Murdered in a Cowardly Manner by Vigilantes."
The Abilene, Great Bend, Dodge City and Iola papers ran a shortened text under "Murdered by Vigilantes" that dropped the editorial close.

Elsewhere it shrank to a line, as in the Martinsburg Herald, which placed the killing "near Belvidere," and the Indiana State Sentinel's column of news items, where the brief was cut off at the foot of the column.
Every version was sympathetic to the victims and hostile to the vigilantes, and none offered the band's side.

accounts.label: Belvidere wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Ashley and Grove, on a hunting and prospecting trip with two women, were met by vigilantes below Englewood; Grove was hanged and Ashley shot dead after he opened fire; the sheriff found no trace of the party.

framing.detail: The dispatch called it 'the most atrocious deed' in 'a country where crime has full sway' and said the vigilantes were worse than those they sought to kill.
Kansas headlines read 'Inhuman Vigilants' and 'Two Kansas Men Murdered in a Cowardly Manner by Vigilantes'; Springfield called Ashley 'an Estimable Citizen'.
The Illinois Staats-Zeitung called the killers a 'Mörderbande' that styled themselves vigilantes.
Several Kansas weeklies ran a shortened version under 'Murdered by Vigilantes' without the editorial closing lines.
